mcqs.question: Why does a per-day boolean grid (isBooked[vehicleId][date]) scale worse than a sorted-interval structure for checking date-range availability?
options: It wastes memory proportional to fleet size times booking-horizon days, and checking one date range means checking one boolean per day in it, rather than a small number of interval comparisons against a compact per-vehicle interval set
It's actually just as fast — the grid approach is generally preferred in production systems
Boolean grids cannot represent bookings longer than 30 days
Sorted intervals only work for vehicle categories, not individual vehicles
mcqs.explanation: The grid's cost scales with fleet size times the number of days tracked, and a range check costs one boolean read per day in the range. An interval set instead stores only actual bookings and answers overlap with a handful of comparisons. There's no such 30-day limit, and interval sets work at either the vehicle or category level.

mcqs.question: An existing booking runs day 3 to day 7. A candidate reservation runs day 6 to day 10. Why do they conflict?
options: They don't conflict, since the start dates are different
existing.start (3) is before candidate.end (10) and candidate.start (6) is before existing.end (7) — both conditions of the overlap check hold, so the ranges share days 6-7
Any two bookings on the same vehicle always conflict regardless of dates
They only conflict if the exact same day appears as a start date in both
mcqs.explanation: The two-condition overlap test — existing.start < candidate.end and candidate.start < existing.end — is what correctly identifies the shared days 6-7, regardless of the start dates differing. Bookings on the same vehicle only conflict if their ranges actually overlap, and matching start dates isn't the relevant condition.

mcqs.question: Why do most large rental chains lock only a vehicle category at booking time instead of a specific VIN?
options: Because customers generally prefer not knowing which exact car they'll get
Because locking a specific vehicle is technically impossible in a reservation system
A specific-vehicle lock means one delayed return or breakdown turns into a broken promise with no substitute, while a category lock lets any available vehicle in that category cover the reservation
Because category-level locking removes the need for a Branch entity
mcqs.explanation: The operational argument is resilience: a category lock absorbs a single vehicle's delay or breakdown by substituting another in the same category, while a specific-vehicle lock has no fallback. It's not about customer preference, it's entirely possible to lock a specific vehicle, and Branch is still needed regardless.

mcqs.question: Why model duration rate, category multiplier, and late/damage fees as separate components a PricingStrategy combines, instead of one formula covering every case?
options: Separate components always compute a lower total price for the customer
It removes the need for a RentalAgreement entity
A single formula is required by most billing regulations
Adding a new fee type, like a one-way drop fee, means adding a new component instead of editing a monolithic calculation every other fee type also depends on
mcqs.explanation: Composability is the point: new fee types become new components rather than edits to a shared formula that every other fee also relies on. Component pricing doesn't change what customers pay by design, doesn't affect the need for RentalAgreement, and isn't a regulatory requirement.

mcqs.question: Why does checking availability by looping through every Reservation record for a vehicle become a real problem over time?
options: It's fine indefinitely, since date-range overlap checks are always O(1) regardless of list size
As a popular vehicle or category accumulates a season's worth of bookings, every availability check re-scans a growing list instead of using a structure built for this exact query
Reservation records expire automatically after being scanned, causing data loss
It only becomes a problem for one-way rentals
mcqs.explanation: A linear scan's cost grows with the number of existing reservations, which is exactly the failure mode the interval-index structure avoids. Overlap checks are not free regardless of size, scanning doesn't delete records, and the cost applies to any high-volume vehicle or category, not just one-way rentals.
